UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

        PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                   Docket No. ER26-3515-000


          PROTEST AND COMMENTS OF JOINT CONSUMER ADVOCATES


           Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (FERC or

Commission) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 the Delaware Division of the Public

Advocate, District of Columbia Office of People’s Counsel, Illinois Citizens Utility Board,

Office of the Illinois Attorney General, Maryland Office of the People’s Counsel, and New

Jersey Division of Rate Counsel (together, Joint Consumer Advocates or JCA) 2 submit this

protest of and comments on the August 13, 2026, filing by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

(PJM) proposing to establish an Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS) and a Large

Load Registry. 3 While JCA appreciate PJM’s efforts in developing and presenting IRAS,

and acknowledge that it is a better outcome than potential alternatives, the proposal falls

short of the just and reasonable standard.

           For the reasons stated below, the Commission should find PJM’s proposal unjust

and unreasonable, and direct PJM to file an amended version of IRAS. PJM has consented

to the Commission’s modification or severing of this proposal to the extent “consistent with

PJM’s overarching objectives in this filing.” 4 To the extent this consent is insufficient to

We note that the Commission’s June 2026 Show Cause Order 6 found PJM’s Open Access

               The Commission should reject PJM’s treatment of IRAS as a compensable resource

should also direct PJM to revise the proposal and modify the new large load self-supply

not previously cleared a prior Base Residual Auction (BRA) are eligible. In addition, the

Commission should direct modification of the proposal to require its review and validation

of data supplied for the Large Load Registry, and to expand access to the information in

the Registry such that the JCA can review the data. Finally, Commission acceptance of the

revised IRAS proposal should be coordinated with the disposition—and rejection—of the

separate Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP) proceeding pending in Docket

No. ER26-3380. 8

                                             SUMMARY

           The instant proposal and PJM’s separate RBP initiative address the same reliability

problem: unprecedented growth in new large loads—chiefly, data centers—that has

outpaced new generation and transmission development and produced consecutive years

of capacity shortfalls in PJM’s BRAs.9 RBP seeks to cover the immediate shortfall, though

does so by means that are unjust and unreasonable in myriad ways. 10 IRAS also seeks to

preserve regional reliability in the face of an unprecedented resource adequacy challenge.

The mechanism facilitates the interconnection of new large loads but requires (or should

require) that they make a choice: either bring new capacity sufficient to meet their needs

or (assuming appropriate state action) face curtailment when circumstances necessitate

load reductions.

           Joint Consumer Advocates recognize and appreciate that PJM’s IRAS proposal

seeks to navigate a difficult course, and we support the general thrust of the proposal. If

implemented correctly, the approach could go far toward maintaining reliability without

either stopping the interconnection of non-capacity backed new large loads or socializing

the reliability consequences of non-capacity backed large-load growth. We submit that

neither of those options was likely to gain regulatory traction or, even more importantly, to

be consistent with PJM’s obligation to ensure resource adequacy. 11 IRAS rightly strikes a

what it discussed with stakeholders and falls short of being just and reasonable in important

respects. In short, and as reviewed in the first part of this pleading, PJM’s basic concept is

largely sound and potentially beneficial. But, as explained in the second part of the

pleading, PJM’s proposed implementation is flawed.

         The flaws include that PJM’s proposal fails to capture all the new large load that

should be a curtailable IRAS resource. PJM exempts new large loads from IRAS to the

extent that they bring their own new capacity but fails to ensure that the “new” capacity in

fact adds to the system’s existing capacity. As explained below, PJM’s proposal would

allow a new large load to decrease its IRAS service (and curtailment risk) by procuring

capacity that already has cleared in previous BRAs. This would increase the amount of

load on the system without either increasing system supply or making the new load an

IRAS resource subject to curtailment. That is an unjust and unreasonable loophole.

         Second, PJM’s proposal to compensate IRAS resources when they are curtailed has

not been shown to be just and reasonable. The compensation proposal departs from the

“connect and manage” proposal it promoted during the stakeholder process, under which

non-capacity backed new large loads would be required to take non-firm transmission

service akin to the approaches adopted and approved in the Southwest Power Pool (SPP)

and Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT). 12 “Connect and manage” was

curtailed. Instead, by declaring that new large loads will be taking firm transmission

service 14 and will be paid for whatever load curtailments are ordered as a form of

         Importantly, IRAS itself does not guarantee that any required curtailments will

necessarily fall on large loads. PJM proposes to issue curtailment directives to Electric

Distribution Companies (EDCs) in the amount of their IRAS load but leaves specific load

curtailments to the state and/or Retail Electric Regulatory Rate Authority (RERRA). 16 And

and made available to regulatory authorities, including ratepayer advocates. Finally, IRAS

does not purport to address other, significant issues, including the increased transmission

or energy costs that result from new large loads, which should also be their cost

responsibility. 17

        In short, when considered in context and against alternatives, IRAS is a flawed step

forward. The Commission can and should take steps to modify the proposal. FERC should

exercise its FPA sections 205 and/or 206 authority and find IRAS unjust and unreasonable

as a compensatory resource adequacy measure. PJM should instead be directed to resubmit

IRAS as requiring non-capacity backed new large loads to take non-firm transmission

service. Indeed, PJM’s tariff already contains non-firm transmission services that appear

consistent with the proposed curtailment priority to be accorded IRAS. 18 Finally,

acceptance of an amended IRAS proposal as urged here renders PJM’s proposed RBP

duplicative and unnecessary. The Commission should couple acceptance of an amended

IRAS proposal with the rejection of the RBP.

                             PROTEST AND COMMENTS

I.      IF PROPERLY IMPLEMENTED, IRAS COULD INSULATE
        RATEPAYERS FROM THE CAPACITY COSTS OF SERVING
        PROJECTED NEW LARGE LOADS BY REMOVING THOSE
        LOADS FROM THE BRA.

                 capacity that serves the broader public by increasing supply.

largest concentration of data center load in the world.” 23 Of the 32 gigawatts (GW) in

margin that would otherwise stand between normal system operations and an emergency.

A new large load that adds to peak demand without contributing commensurate new

capacity exacerbates PJM’s current and projected capacity shortfall and increases the risk

that PJM will be forced to shed load to maintain system reliability. 25 As that shortfall

increases, the risk of load-shedding increases correspondingly. Left unaddressed, continued

large load growth would progressively erode the reliability margin on which existing

customers rely.

           The stress on PJM’s capacity market is driven by the unique phenomenon of new

large data center load—real and projected—that is unlike the diffuse, organic load growth

typical of the U.S. electric industry since its inception. The Commission recognizes that

large loads are “a separate category of load” and has directed every RTO/Independent

System Operator (ISO), including PJM, to define “large load” in their respective tariffs—

because, among other considerations, their integration “poses specific challenges to

transmission system operation given their size, operational behavior, and unique potential

to impact the transmission system.” 26

customers. The key to this safeguard is the accompanying removal of IRAS load from the

Interconnecting large load customers that cause the need for network upgrades or system

stress are “differently situated” from customers whose presence on the system causes no

framework—through reserve-margin planning, capacity-market procurement, and the

reliability-coordination function PJM has performed for decades. The present shortfall does

not arise from any change in that existing load’s behavior; it arises from rapid incremental

demand growth that is materially different in scale and timing from anything the framework

has previously accommodated. 29 Removing from the BRA the loads that caused the

II.        IRAS SHOULD HELP EASE THE DEMAND PRESSURES
           PLAGUING THE BRA.

           In planning and administering the regional transmission system, PJM seeks “to

meet the demands for firm transmission service, and to support competition, in the PJM

Region.” 41 The misalignment of supply and demand driven by projected new large loads

is an impediment to competition. In a supply-constrained market, new entry cannot perform

its function of disciplining the market power of incumbent resources: 42

                    [C]ontinuing to simply accept the interconnection of large
                    data center loads that cannot be served reliably because there
                    is not adequate dispatchable capacity, is not a reasonable
                    path forward and is not an efficient or competitive market
                    solution and is not a solution of any kind. That path leads to
                    continued shortfalls, increased reliability issues, continued
                    maximum prices, and continued calls to abandon markets. 43

           The answer is not to throw out the BRA baby with the new large load bathwater.

“[C]urrent data center issues [should not be] a pretext for redefining fundamental elements

of the PJM market design.” 44 PJM’s IRAS proposal offers an (albeit flawed) market-based

solution for new large loads that seek to connect to the grid while providing a pathway for
